title: WHAT IF YOU FLEW TO MARS
ON A NUCLEAR REACTOR?

sets.ship: NASA's SR-1 Freedom spacecraft big in frame in deep space, Jump treatment. far: deep-navy starfield with slow light rays and a planet disc per setp.bg; mid: the ship: silver box-shaped central body (Power and Propulsion Element), two long purple-and-white checkered roll-out solar array wings, two grey finned radiator panels, a SHORT metal boom at the front ending in a squat cylindrical reactor module behind a dark round shield disc, a white X-band dish, a Hall thruster nozzle at the back, all with 4 px dark outlines and an orange rim light; near: a few out-of-focus dust motes drifting past. setp.t 0..1 = slow camera drift along the ship; setp.reactor 0..1 = the reactor module glows from dark to warm orange with a pulsing bloom and heat shimmer from the radiators; setp.thrust 0..1 = a soft blue plume streams out of the thruster; setp.arrays 0..1 = the solar wings unroll from tight rolls to full length and catch a gold sun glint; setp.bg 'stars'|'earth'|'mars' = a big Earth limb lower-left, a big Mars disc right, or stars only; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.cutaway: A clean labelled cutaway diagram of SR-1 Freedom on a dark navy blueprint grid, side view, flat vector with 4 px outlines: from left to right the reactor module, the short boom, the grey radiator panels, the silver Power and Propulsion Element body with the purple-and-white solar array wings folded above and below, the Hall thruster at the back, and a small capsule marked as the SkyFall payload tucked under the body. setp.hl 0..5 = which part is highlighted with a gold outline glow and a short cream leader line (0 reactor, 1 boom, 2 radiators, 3 body, 4 thruster, 5 SkyFall capsule); setp.boom 0..1 = the boom length morphs from long (0, early design) to short (1, new design) with the reactor sliding closer; setp.t 0..1 = slow push; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.control: Mission control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Jump treatment. far: dark room with a huge wall screen showing a simple outlined SR-1 schematic and a rising power line graph, soft screen glow and light rays; mid: two rows of outlined consoles with glowing cream and cyan screens, two empty operator chairs side by side at the front console; near: an out-of-focus console edge and a coffee mug silhouette sliding past the bottom-left. setp.power 0..1 = the graph line on the wall screen climbs in steps and a big round power gauge on the screen fills; setp.alarm 0..1 = the room light shifts toward a red tint; setp.t 0..1 = slow dolly; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.core: Inside the reactor and power system, stylised flat vector on deep navy. Left: a squat outlined reactor vessel with a glowing orange core; centre: a closed loop pipe (gas loop) carrying little orange heat arrows clockwise to a round outlined turbine wheel; right: a generator box throwing small cyan electricity bolts out along a cable; top: grey radiator fins on the loop dumping heat as rising red shimmer. setp.power 0..1 = core glow, arrow speed and turbine spin; setp.heat 0..1 = how red the radiator fins glow; setp.elec 0..1 = how many cyan bolts flow out; setp.t 0..1 = slow push; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.pad: A rocket launch at dawn on a Florida coast pad, Jump treatment: far: pink-orange sky with light rays over the sea; mid: a tall white outlined rocket on a grey launch tower with steam clouds at its base; near: dark palm and fence silhouettes sliding past. setp.lift 0..1 = engines ignite (0.2) with a bright orange-white flame and billowing cream smoke, then the rocket climbs up and out of frame with a long trail (1); setp.shake 0..1 = camera shake amount; setp.glow 'gold'|'red'.
sets.orbit: Leaving Earth: a huge curved blue Earth limb filling the lower part of the frame with white clouds and a thin cyan atmosphere glow, black-navy space above with stars; the small SR-1 Freedom ship (as the sr1 icon, bigger) climbs away up-right on a dotted gold escape curve. setp.leave 0..1 = the ship moves along the curve and Earth shrinks and drops away; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.route: A flat top-down map of the inner solar system on deep navy: a bright Sun in the centre, the thin outlined orbits of Earth and Mars as circles with the planets as small outlined balls, and a long dotted gold transfer arc from Earth to Mars with a tiny ship icon on it. setp.prog 0..1 = the ship moves along the arc leaving a solid trail; setp.mode 'nuclear'|'solar' = trail colour orange-red (nuclear) or gold-yellow (solar), with a small matching icon (atom or sun) riding above the ship; setp.t 0..1 = slow zoom; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.mars: Arriving at Mars, Jump treatment: a huge rusty-red Mars disc fills the right two-thirds with craters, the Valles Marineris canyon and a thin pink atmosphere glow; deep space and stars on the left; the SR-1 Freedom ship small in the upper left. setp.drop 0..1 = a small cone-shaped capsule leaves the ship and falls toward Mars, its heat shield glowing orange-white with a plasma trail (0.5-1); setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.glow 'gold'|'red'.
sets.sky: High in the pink-tan Martian sky over red dunes and layered cliffs, Jump treatment with a small pale Sun: a falling capsule above opens and three Ingenuity-style helicopters drop out, unfold their legs and blades and spin up into flight. far: hazy cliffs and dunes with dust haze; mid: the helicopters and capsule; near: blowing dust streaks. setp.deploy 0..1 = 0 capsule closed, 0.3 helicopters drop out folded, 0.6 they unfold, 1 all three fly with spinning blurred rotors; setp.t 0..1 = slow pan; setp.glow 'gold'|'red'.
sets.ground: Martian landscape seen in a cross-section: above, rusty plains and a cliff with three Ingenuity-style helicopters hovering in a line with spinning rotors; below the surface line, layered red-brown rock strata in a cut-away. setp.radar 0..1 = cyan radar wave arcs pulse down from each helicopter into the ground; setp.ice 0..1 = a glowing pale-blue ice layer appears under the ground with a depth bracket; setp.wind 0..1 = dust streaks and a small wind sock show the wind; setp.t 0..1 = slow pan; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.moonbase: A small Moon base at night on the grey lunar surface, Jump treatment: far: black sky with stars and a small blue Earth; mid: two white outlined habitat domes with warm windows and a compact cylindrical fission reactor unit on a stand a short way off with grey radiator fins, cables to the domes; near: grey regolith rocks sliding past. setp.night 0..1 = darkness level (sunlit grey at 0, deep night at 1); setp.lights 0..1 = the reactor glows and the dome windows and floodlights stay lit warm gold; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.rail: The railroad of the solar system: a stylised flat-vector railway track (cream rails, dark sleepers, 4 px outlines) laid across deep space from a small Earth on the left, past the Moon, to Mars, then fading on toward a far ringed Saturn; a small SR-1 Freedom ship rides the first stretch like a freight engine. setp.lay 0..1 = how far the track has been laid (it builds piece by piece from Earth); setp.t 0..1 = the ship moves along the laid track; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.sr1: Small icon of NASA's SR-1 Freedom spacecraft: a silver box-shaped central body, two long purple-and-white checkered roll-out solar array wings, two grey radiator panels, a short metal boom ending in a squat cylindrical reactor module with a dark shield disc, and a soft blue thruster glow at the back, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true makes the reactor module glow warm orange.
props.heli: Mars helicopter icon in the Ingenuity style: a small grey cube body, two stacked counter-rotating dark rotor blades on a mast, a small square solar panel on top, four thin splayed legs, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.spin true blurs the rotors into spinning discs with motion lines; pp.folded true shows the legs and blades folded tight like a packed toy.

props.badge: Outlined cream ID badge on a lanyard with a blank face-less avatar square and pp.text in FONTS.ui (max 6 chars) in bold; pp.color gold|cyan sets the lanyard colour; pp.s scale.
props.switch: Big outlined toggle switch on a dark panel, cream lever with a red tip; it flips from OFF to ON at p 0.4 with a small green lamp lighting up; pp.s scale.

film.vo: You are strapped beside a nuclear reactor, deep in space.
And someone in Houston is about to switch it on.
Two operators sit side by side at the controls.
One from NASA. One from the Department of Energy.
Waking this reactor takes about seven days, one careful step at a time.
This is S R One Freedom.
film.dir: proud, a beat of reveal; stress 'Freedom'

film.vo: The first fission-powered spacecraft ever to leave Earth orbit.
NASA locked in its design this week. Launch: late twenty twenty-eight.
So what if you rode along, all the way to Mars?
First, the bad news. There are no seats.
It is a robot ship. Nobody planned for a passenger.
So you squeeze in next to its real cargo: three folded helicopters.
Rule one: you go where the ship goes. No turning back.
Rule two: when the reactor runs, you stay behind the shield.
Rule three: pack snacks. Mars is a long way off.
And the strangest rule? This nuclear ship barely flies on nuclear power.
Hold that thought. First, the tour.
Freedom weighs about twelve thousand kilograms.
That is roughly two big elephants, in space.
Up front sits the reactor, on a metal arm called the boom.
Early drawings had a long boom, to keep radiation far away.
This week's news: the boom just got shorter.
Better shielding lets the reactor sit closer to the ship.
Shorter means lighter, and simpler to build.
Shorter boom. Same legroom. Which is none.
Behind you is the main body: the Power and Propulsion Element.
Its wings are giant roll-out solar arrays, purple and white.
Grey radiator panels stick out to dump the reactor's heat.
And bigger dishes, to talk to Earth across deep space.
At the back: a Hall thruster, rated at twelve kilowatts.
It doesn't burn fuel like a rocket. It runs on electricity.
Which raises a question. Where does all that electricity come from?
Launch day, late twenty twenty-eight. You're tucked inside a rocket.
Right now, the reactor is switched off. It stays off through launch.
Its fuel is uranium, but a special kind.
High-assay low-enriched uranium. Engineers call it hay-loo.
Three. Two. One. Liftoff!
The rocket shakes. You shake. The helicopters stay packed tight.
Minutes later, the rocket lets go. You're on your own.
Freedom heads out on an Earth escape path, aimed at Mars.
Then the big moment arrives. Time to wake the reactor.
Once Freedom has left Earth orbit, Houston starts the reactor.
No big lever. Power creeps up, a little at a time.
Inside, uranium atoms split apart and give off heat.
That heat is the whole point. It's where the power comes from.
A loop of gas carries the heat to a spinning turbine.
Engineers call it a closed Brayton cycle. Heat in, electricity out.
The design target: twenty kilowatts of electricity.
Enough to light two hundred old hundred-watt bulbs at once.
But a reactor makes much more heat than electricity.
And in space, there's no air to carry that heat away.
So the radiators glow, shedding heat into the dark.
NASA just awarded thirty-nine point three million dollars for that cooling system.
film.dir: newsy, weighty; stress 'thirty-nine point three million'

film.vo: Johns Hopkins' Applied Physics Lab will build it, with heat pipes and radiators.
Seven days of checks later, the reactor is humming.
You're riding the first fission-powered ship ever beyond Earth orbit.
Now that electricity flows to the thruster.
The Hall thruster lights up with a soft blue glow.
It fires charged gas out the back. Very, very fast.
But the push is gentle. Barely a whisper.
You wouldn't even feel it. Your sandwich wouldn't slide off its tray.
But it never gets tired.
It can keep pushing for a very long time.
A chemical rocket is a sprint. This is a marathon.
Reactor power driving electric thrusters. That's nuclear electric propulsion.
Nobody has ever flown it in deep space before.
And then... the reactor shuts down.
Remember the strange rule? Here it is.
For most of the trip to Mars, Freedom cruises on sunlight.
The nuclear spaceship is mostly solar powered on the way there.
So why build a reactor, then switch it off?
Because the first job is to learn.
Start it, run it, shut it down. Then send every reading home.
Nobody has done this beyond Earth orbit. Every number is new.
So the solar arrays take over.
The main body can make forty-eight kilowatts of power.
Yes. On this trip, sunlight out-powers the reactor. For now.
Mars is far. The ship follows a long curve around the Sun.
Days become weeks. Weeks become months.
You count the stars. You run out of snacks.
So you name the helicopters. Rotor, Blade, and Steve.
Up ahead, a small red dot is slowly getting bigger.
That's Mars. And it's time to make a delivery.
Your cargo has a name: SkyFall.
A capsule holding three helicopters, evolved from Ingenuity.
Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
These three are its bigger, bolder grandkids.
Freedom lets the capsule go, toward Mars.
It plunges into the thin Martian air, heat shield glowing.
Then the wild part: the helicopters deploy in mid-air.
No landing pad. No runway. They unfold, spin up, and fly.
Rotor, Blade, and Steve are airborne!
Each carries ground-penetrating radar, and cameras.
They measure air temperature, wind speed, and wind direction.
Their big job: hunt for ice hidden under the ground.
If they find it, the radar can help show how deep it goes.
Ice means water. Future explorers will want every drop.
Delivery complete. But Freedom isn't finished yet.
With the cargo gone, Freedom restarts its reactor.
This time, there's no precious cargo to protect.
The reactor team says now they can really drive it.
They even plan to make some parts fail, on purpose.
Why break your own ship? To learn before people depend on it.
Every reading beams home through those bigger dishes.
To NASA's Deep Space Network, back on Earth.
But only so much data can squeeze through. So every bit counts.
How long will the reactor run? Even NASA hasn't decided yet.
Its power level and number of radiators are still being worked out.
So why does any of this matter?
Far from the Sun, sunlight gets weak. And at night, it's gone.
A reactor doesn't care. It keeps running in the dark.
Next comes Lunar Reactor One, to power NASA's Moon Base.
Through the long lunar nights, when solar panels go quiet.
And one day, ships that reach the outer solar system.
NASA's program director has a name for this mission.
The first freight run on the railroad of the solar system.
Freedom lays the very first stretch of track.
So back to that moment. Houston wakes the reactor, step by step.
And you're beside it, heading for Mars on sunlight and uranium.
Three helicopters. One reactor. A seven-day wake-up. Zero seats.
The age of nuclear spaceships starts with a robot and a delivery.
Would you ride along, or wait for the version with seats?
Tell me in the comments.
Tomorrow: what if you flew a helicopter on Titan?

short.vo: This spaceship carries a nuclear reactor to Mars.
NASA just locked in its design. Launch: late twenty twenty-eight.
Here's the twist. The reactor barely flies the ship.
Houston wakes it up slowly, over about seven days.
It makes twenty kilowatts and powers a blue electric thruster.
Then it shuts down. Sunlight flies it most of the way.
Why? The first job is to learn: start, run, stop, in deep space.
At Mars, it drops a capsule with three helicopters.
They unfold in mid-air, then hunt for ice underground.
Then the reactor restarts, and engineers push it hard.
They even plan to break parts on purpose, to learn.
Because one day, reactors will light Moon bases through the long night.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: a helicopter on Titan.
And it all starts with one ship.
